name: Urolithin A
lead: Urolithin A is a compound formed in the gut when bacteria transform ellagic acid and ellagitannins, polyphenols found in pomegranates, walnuts, raspberries, strawberries, tea and oak-aged wine [1]. It is not known to occur in any food itself, and how much a person makes depends on their gut microbiota; some people convert these precursors efficiently, others barely at all [1][2]. Supplements that deliver urolithin A directly, the best known being a branded form called Mitopure, are sold for muscle, mitochondrial and healthy-ageing support [3][4].

For appearance, the case people make is indirect and runs through the body rather than the skin. Muscle is a large part of how a physique reads, and urolithin A has been tested in randomised trials for muscle endurance and strength in middle-aged and older adults. The chain readers describe is: supplement, then support for the cellular recycling of worn mitochondria (mitophagy), then better muscle endurance and recovery capacity, then more productive training and a better-maintained physique with age [3][6][9][10]. Companies and some researchers also discuss mitochondrial health in skin, and a 2026 laboratory paper on topical urolithin A in skin cells has appeared [35].

Urolithin A was identified as a mitophagy inducer in worms and rodents in 2016 [5]. A first-in-human safety trial followed in 2019 [7], randomised trials reporting muscle outcomes in 2022 [3][6], a systematic review in 2024 [8] and an immune-ageing trial in 2025 [17]. Several of these were run with the supplier's involvement, which reviews note [8][7]. In training forums it is discussed alongside NAD+ precursors, CoQ10, PQQ and fisetin [9][10][11].

chain: Take urolithin A directly, bypassing variable gut conversion
Mitophagy and mitochondrial markers shift in muscle
Reported gains in muscle endurance or strength in trials
Better sustained training and a maintained physique with age
angle.text: Urolithin A is used by people who want to keep muscle quality and training capacity as they age. In trials, muscle endurance and in one trial hamstring strength improved versus placebo, which is the route by which it connects to physique. Skin and facial effects have been examined only in early laboratory work.

paras: Urolithins are a family of metabolites. A 2022 review counted 13 urolithins and their conjugates described in humans, found in urine, blood, faeces, breast milk and some tissues [14]. Urolithin A is the one that has drawn commercial and research attention, because it was the compound found to stimulate mitophagy, the selective removal and recycling of damaged mitochondria [5][15].

Mitochondria are the cell's energy-producing organelles, and researchers in ageing biology link declining mitochondrial quality to loss of muscle function with age [15][34]. Proponents of urolithin A describe it as a way to support that housekeeping process. Reviews describe the idea as promising and still developing, with the human data concentrated in a small number of trials [8][15].

Ellagitannins from plants are hydrolysed in the gut to release ellagic acid, which gut bacteria then convert to urolithins by removing one of two lactone rings and then stripping hydroxyl groups one at a time. Gordonibacter urolithinfaciens and G. pamelaeae contribute, and Enterocloster species carry an enzyme that converts urolithin C to urolithin A; the full set of organisms involved is not settled [1].

People fall into urolithin metabotypes. Intervention trials consistently observe three patterns, usually labelled UM-A, UM-B and UM-0, and these patterns appear independent of food source, age and health status [2][13][14]. This variability is the rationale given for taking urolithin A directly rather than relying on pomegranate or nuts [3][1].

After absorption, urolithin A is conjugated in intestinal and liver cells and circulates mainly as glucuronide and sulfate forms, which are excreted in urine [1]. Its chemical name is 3,8-dihydroxy-6H-dibenzo[b,d]pyran-6-one [1].

Urolithins were first described in animal and human metabolism work decades ago; the Trends in Molecular Medicine review notes urolithin A was discovered about 40 years ago but only recently explored for ageing and disease [15]. Later work described the urolithin metabotypes in humans, as summarised in reviews [13][14].

The step that brought it to wider attention was a 2016 Nature Medicine paper by Ryu, Auwerx and colleagues. They reported that urolithin A induced mitophagy in cells and animals after oral intake, preserved mitochondrial respiration and mobility and extended lifespan in the roundworm C. elegans, and improved exercise capacity in two mouse models of age-related muscle decline and in young rats [5][35]. The consumer brand Timeline describes its Mitopure product as born from research at EPFL [33].

In 2018 the US FDA's GRAS inventory recorded a notice (GRN 791) for urolithin A as a food ingredient at 250 mg to 1 g per serving, as described by Wikipedia [1]. The first-in-human trial, by Andreux and colleagues, appeared in Nature Metabolism in 2019 [7]. Randomised trials in middle-aged and older adults followed in 2022 [3][6].

Urolithin A is not sold on an established appearance claim in the trial literature. The appearance-relevant links are muscle and, more speculatively, skin. For muscle, people describe using it to support muscle endurance and recovery capacity as they get older, so they can keep training hard [9][10][11]. The Timeline site, which sells a branded product, states strength and mitochondrial-renewal claims, lists skin among the systems influenced by mitochondrial health, and carries the standard disclaimer that statements are not FDA-evaluated [33].

On skin, the only item found in a literature search was a 2026 iScience laboratory paper titled as topical urolithin A activating mitophagy and promoting skin longevity; no human skin-appearance trial was found [35]. T Nation writers describe it as a longevity supplement for lifters rather than a cosmetic [16][11].

Human studies have examined muscle endurance in older adults, muscle strength and exercise performance in middle-aged adults, and immune ageing [3][6][17]. Registered studies address COPD rehabilitation, glucose metabolism, obesity, frailty and Alzheimer's disease [18][19][20][21][22].

Urolithin A is proposed to stimulate mitophagy through the PINK1/Parkin pathway, clearing damaged mitochondria so that healthier ones replace them, and to reduce detrimental inflammation [12][15]. A 2025 review contrasted it with spermidine, which acts on autophagy through AMPK and sirtuin 1 signalling, saying the two overlap in part but are not identical [12].

Other reported actions come from laboratory and animal work: strengthening of gut barrier integrity through the Nrf2 pathway, improved cognition and restored mitophagy in Alzheimer's disease models, and protection of the retina in an acute neurodegeneration model through p62-dependent lysophagy [23][24][25].

Company-registered studies have compared bioavailability of different Mitopure formulations in healthy adults [4][26][27][28]. Timeline states that its product delivers several times more urolithin A than a serving of pomegranate juice [33].

First-in-human safety trial (2019). Andreux and colleagues gave urolithin A to healthy, sedentary older adults, either as a single dose or as repeated doses for four weeks. The primary outcome, safety, was favourable. The compound appeared in plasma at all doses tested, and at the two higher repeated doses plasma acylcarnitines and expression of mitochondrial genes in skeletal muscle changed in a pattern the authors described as improved mitochondrial and cellular health [7].

Older adults (JAMA Network Open, 2022). A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Seattle randomised 66 adults aged 65 to 90 to urolithin A (33) or placebo (33) for four months. The two primary outcomes, change in six-minute walk distance and maximal ATP production in a hand muscle, did not differ significantly between groups; walk distance rose by 60.8 m with urolithin A and 42.5 m with placebo. Secondary outcomes showed improved endurance in the hand and leg muscles tested at two months, and lower levels of some acylcarnitines, ceramides and C-reactive protein at four months. No significant difference in adverse events was found [6].

Middle-aged adults (Cell Reports Medicine, 2022). A randomised, placebo-controlled trial gave urolithin A at two doses for four months and reported about a 12 percent improvement in muscle strength, clinically meaningful gains in peak oxygen consumption and the six-minute walk test, and lower plasma acylcarnitines and C-reactive protein, along with higher muscle expression of mitophagy- and mitochondria-related proteins. The primary endpoint, peak power output, did not improve significantly [3]. Timeline's site describes the strength result as a hamstring measure in sedentary adults with an average BMI near 30 [33].

Immune ageing (Nature Aging, 2025). A randomised, double-blind trial in 50 healthy middle-aged adults gave urolithin A or placebo for four weeks. It reported an expansion of naive-like, less exhausted CD8 T cells and higher fatty-acid oxidation capacity in these cells, plus changes in natural killer cells and monocytes. An erratum has since been published [17].

Systematic review (2024). A review pooled five studies in 250 healthy people given between 10 and 1,000 mg per day for 28 days to four months. It reported dose-dependent anti-inflammatory effects and upregulation of some mitochondrial genes and autophagy and fatty-acid-oxidation markers. It found no effect on maximal mitochondrial ATP production, mitochondrial biogenesis, dynamics or gut microbiota composition, and increased muscle strength and endurance, with no effect on anthropometrics, cardiovascular outcomes or physical function. Adverse events were mild or moderate and judged unrelated [8].

Several trials were conducted with the supplement's developer, which authors of the 2024 review and others note when discussing the evidence base [8][7]. Reviews state that longer interventions and more physiological systems need to be studied [8]. Registered trials listed on ClinicalTrials.gov include studies in obesity, frailty, Alzheimer's disease, COPD and glucose metabolism [18][19][20][21][22].

Wikipedia reports that in vivo studies found no toxicity or specific adverse effects from dietary urolithin A, and that safety studies in older people showed good tolerability [1]. The first-in-human trial listed a favourable safety profile as its primary result [7], the 2022 JAMA Network Open trial found no significant difference in adverse events from placebo [6], and the systematic review described adverse events as mild or moderate [8]. Long-term safety data are limited, and trials have been in healthy adults rather than pregnant people or children [8]. The FDA GRAS notice covers specified serving amounts as a food ingredient [1].

In forums, urolithin A sits in the longevity-supplement corner of training culture. On T Nation, users list Mitopure in pre-workout stacks, recommend it alongside NAD+, PQQ and fisetin for mitochondrial repair, and discuss cost, with one user noting a branded product at over 110 dollars for 30 days [29][9][10]. A 77-year-old user reported strength gains while taking it with NAD+, which is anecdotal [11]. Site articles promote pomegranate-derived punicalagins as precursors, describing circulation, sexual and cognitive benefits [30][31][32].

Mitopure is sold by Timeline, which states that it has completed more than 25 human clinical trials and holds GRAS status; the company's own materials are the source for those figures [33]. Companion topics are other autophagy activators such as spermidine, covered in a 2025 review [12].

lore.intro: Urolithin A is discussed in training forums as a mitochondrial repair supplement for muscle and ageing, often named alongside NAD+ precursors, PQQ and CoQ10 [9][10].

claims.claim: Urolithin A repairs mitochondria and improves muscle
claims.believers: Users cite podcasters and report strength gains at the doses used in trials [10][11].
claims.experts: Randomised trials report improved strength or endurance in some measures and no difference in others, and reviews note small samples and sponsor involvement [3][6][8].

claims.claim: Pomegranate or ellagitannin foods give the same benefit
claims.believers: T Nation articles promote pomegranate extracts and punicalagins as precursors [30][31].
claims.experts: Conversion depends on gut microbiota, and some people produce little or no urolithin A [1][2][13].

claims.claim: It improves sexual health and brain function
claims.believers: Articles attribute improved blood flow, learning and memory to punicalagin-derived urolithin A [30][31].
claims.experts: Alzheimer's disease models show effects in animals, and a registered Alzheimer's trial exists, but no cited human trial establishes sexual or cognitive benefit [24][22].

claims.claim: It makes you look younger by renewing mitochondria in skin
claims.believers: Brand materials list skin among the systems that depend on mitochondrial health [33].
claims.experts: Skin work found in the literature is laboratory research on topical application; no human skin-appearance trial was located [35].

claims.claim: A daily supplement can substitute for exercise in older age
claims.believers: Some forum users describe it as a way to keep strength when training is limited [11].
claims.experts: Trial authors tested it in addition to usual routines, with improvements in some endurance and strength measures and no change in others; exercise remains the primary intervention in a Sports Medicine review of mitochondrial targets [3][6][34].
